summary: A 1970 response to RFC 28 on time standards. It discusses the IMP's timing: a fine-grained hardware clock used for internal events, such as tracing, and a coarser software clock used for most measurements.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a reply that says which clocks inside the network boxes are used to time things, and how finely they tick.

subtitle: The IMP uses two clocks: a fine hardware clock for internal timing and a coarser software clock for measurements.

tldr.problem: RFC 28 raised questions about time standards for network measurements.
tldr.mechanism: The IMP contains a 16-bit hardware clock incremented every 100 microseconds for internal timing and tracing. A separate 25.6 millisecond software clock is used for most network measurements.
tldr.outcome: This two-tier timing approach resolved the timing requirements for early ARPANET operations.

today: RFC 29 documents early timing requirements for the ARPANET. Modern networks use far more precise timing for measurement and synchronization.

sections.title: Network Timing
sections.content: RFC 29 responds to Bill English's RFC 28 questions about time standards. A millisecond clock is satisfactory for most network measurements, since round-trip message transit times are typically at least tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring how long messages take does not need very precise timing—a millisecond is good enough.

sections.title: Hardware Clock
sections.content: The IMP contains a 16-bit hardware clock that is incremented every 100 microseconds. This fine-grained clock allows for precise timing of internal events within the IMP, such as during tracing and internal event sequencing. The hardware clock provides microsecond-level granularity for debugging and understanding the IMP's internal behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The IMP's fast clock ticks every 100 millionths of a second, which is fast enough to time internal events.

sections.title: Software Clock for Measurements
sections.content: Most network measurements use a coarser 25.6 millisecond software clock. This granularity is adequate because round-trip message transit times are typically at least tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Using a software clock for measurements reduces the processing burden on the IMP compared to using the hardware clock for every measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: A slow clock that ticks every 25 milliseconds is accurate enough for measuring message delays across the network.
